doc_name: Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002
text: The Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002, informally known as the Iraq Resolution, was a joint resolution passed by the United States Congress in October 2002 as Public Law No. 107-243, authorizing the use of the United States Armed Forces against Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist Iraqi government in what would become Operation Iraqi Freedom. The resolution cited several justifications for military action, including support and encouragement of diplomatic efforts by President George W. Bush to strictly enforce through the U.N. Security Council all relevant Security Council resolutions regarding Iraq and to obtain prompt and decisive action to ensure Iraq abandoned its strategy of delay, evasion, and noncompliance and promptly complied with all such resolutions. It authorized President Bush to use U.S. Armed Forces "as he determines to be necessary and appropriate" to defend national security against the continuing threat from Iraq and to enforce all relevant U.N. Security Council Resolutions on Iraq. President Bush sought congressional authorization shortly after his September 12, 2002 statement before the U.N. General Assembly requesting swift Security Council action. Among the legislative proposals introduced in response, S.J.Res. 45 (Senators Daschle and Lott), H.J.Res. 114 (Rep. Hastert and Rep. Gephardt), and S.J.Res. 46 (Sen. Lieberman) were based on or modified from the White House proposal, while H.J.Res. 110 (Rep. Hastings) was a separate proposal never considered on the floor. Ultimately, the Hastert–Gephardt proposal became the focus of congressional action. Introduced on October 2, 2002, H.J.Res. 114 passed the House on October 10, 2002, by a vote of 296–133, and the Senate on October 11, 2002, by a vote of 77–23, and was signed into law as Pub. L. 107–243 on October 16, 2002. The resolution was supported by a list of senators including Baucus, Bayh, Biden, Breaux, Cantwell, Carnahan, Carper, Cleland, Clinton, Daschle, Dodd, Dorgan, Edwards, Feinstein, Harkin, Hollings, Johnson, Kerry, Kohl, Landrieu, Lieberman, Lincoln, Miller, Nelson (FL and NE), Reid, Rockefeller, Schumer, and Torricelli, as well as Akaka, Bingaman, Boxer, Byrd, Conrad, Corzine, Dayton, Durbin, Feingold, Graham, Inouye, Kennedy, Leahy, Levin, Mikulski, Murray, Reed, Sarbanes, Stabenow, Wellstone, and Wyden. In 2003, the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit refused to review the legality of the invasion, citing a lack of ripeness, and a three-judge panel dismissed the case, stating the judiciary cannot intervene absent a fully developed conflict between the President and Congress or if Congress granted the President "absolute discretion" to declare war. Similar judicial review efforts have been dismissed on various justiciability grounds. United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan stated in 2004 that the invasion was illegal and not in conformity with the UN Charter. Debate over the legality under international law centers on ambiguous language in U.N. Resolution 1441 (2002), which declared Iraq was in "material breach" of the cease-fire under U.N. Resolution 687 (1991), requiring cooperation with weapons inspectors. The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties allows a party to invoke a "material breach" to suspend a multilateral treaty, and the U.S. and U.K. argue that this right enabled them to suspend the cease-fire under Resolution 687 and continue hostilities under the authority of U.N. Resolution 678 (1990), which originally authorized force after Iraq invaded Kuwait—this argument was previously used in Operation Desert Fox in 1998. They also assert that while Resolution 1441 required the Security Council to assess inspector reports, it did not require agreement on action, and if Iraq was found to have breached the resolution, no member state was constrained from acting to defend itself. The U.S. government further claimed the right to pre-emptive self-defense against terrorism fostered by Iraq. It remains unclear whether any party other than the Security Council can determine Iraq's breach of Resolution 1441, as U.N. members argue interpretation and enforcement of resolutions is not the responsibility of a single member. Other nations have maintained that a second resolution was required to initiate hostilities. On June 17, 2021, the House of Representatives voted to repeal the 2002 resolution by a vote of 268–161, with 219 Democrats and 49 Republicans supporting repeal and 160 Republicans and 1 Democrat opposing it. In July 2021, Senators Christopher Murphy, Mike Lee, and Bernie Sanders introduced S.2391, the National Security Powers Act of 2021, to repeal previous war authorizations and establish new procedures, but a Senator placed a quasi-anonymous hold on it in committee, preventing advancement; its House companion, H.R.5410, did not include repeal language and was similarly held in committee. On March 16, 2023, Senators Tim Kaine and Todd Young introduced S.316 to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, which passed the Senate 68–27, but its House companion, H.R.932, was quasi-anonymously held by a Representative in the House Committee on Foreign Affairs since February 9, 2023. On July 13, 2023, Kaine and Young introduced S.Amdt.427 to S.2226, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, to repeal the 1991 and 2002 AUMFs, but failed to propose it on the floor in time, so when the bill passed the Senate, the amendment was not acted upon and was excluded by law. Both AUMFs were ultimately repealed when President Donald Trump signed the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 on December 18, 2025.
